At six in the morning, the city sounds like a giant mechanical animal stirring in its sleep. Buses cough at corners, bicycles whisper over pavement, and somewhere a kettle announces breakfast. I like this hour because the streets possess the unfinished quality of dreams, and even old buildings seem softened by mist.

I often walk without a destination, carrying pastries and questions. Why do some doors have bright numbers while others hide behind ivy? Why does a dog stare at a shadow as if it had betrayed him? Why do people hurry when they are late for something that will begin without them?

Today, I followed a sparrow into a courtyard filled with lemon trees. It hopped from a fountain rim to a blue bowl, paused, and vanished behind leaves. A woman nearby watered herbs, humming a tune. Nothing remarkable happened, yet everything felt briefly complete: water, music, sunlight, the bird’s impatient rustling.

Perhaps happiness is less a destination than an accidental arrival. Perhaps it waits in untended courtyards, in warm bread, in conversations remembered years later. By noon, the city will be loud and crowded, but for now it belongs to shadows, mystery, and people who notice small things.

I sat on a stone bench, ate an almond cookie, and watched the lemon leaves tremble. The sparrow returned carrying a thread in its beak. It looked like an ambassador from a secret country. I decided that today’s purpose would be to receive its message patiently.

Then I went home.

I like this hour because the streets possess the unfinished quality of dreams, and even old buildings seem softened by mist.

I often walk without a destination, carrying pastries and questions. Why do some doors have bright numbers while others hide behind ivy? Why does a dog stare at a shadow as if it had betrayed him? Why do people hurry when they are late for something that will begin without them?

Today, I followed a sparrow into a courtyard filled with lemon trees. It hopped from a fountain rim to a blue bowl, paused, and vanished behind leaves. A woman nearby watered herbs, humming a tune. Nothing remarkable happened, yet everything felt briefly complete: water, music, sunlight, the bird’s impatient rustling.

Perhaps happiness is less a destination than an accidental arrival. Perhaps it waits in untended courtyards, in warm bread, in conversations remembered years later. By noon, the city will be loud and crowded, but for now it belongs to shadows, mystery, and people who notice small things.

I sat on a stone bench, ate an almond cookie, and watched the lemon leaves tremble. The sparrow returned carrying a thread in its beak. It looked like an ambassador from a secret country. I decided that today’s purpose would be to receive its message patiently.

Then I went home.
